concepts.title: Conditional Generative Models for Prediction
concepts.one_liner: Generative models can be used to solve prediction problems by modeling the relationship between inputs and outputs.
concepts.content: Generative models have three primary uses: synthesizing realistic but novel data, learning representations of data, and solving prediction problems. This third use is arguably the most widespread application of generative models in practice.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard regression often fails when there are multiple valid answers for a single input; conditional generative models provide a framework to handle this ambiguity by modeling the full output distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Generative models can synthesize data, learn representations, or solve prediction problems.

slots.motivation: Standard regression often fails when there are multiple valid answers for a single input; conditional generative models provide a framework to handle this ambiguity by modeling the full output distribution.
slots.key_passage: - Generative models can synthesize data, learn representations, or solve prediction problems.

concepts.title: Point Prediction
concepts.one_liner: A point prediction is a single output value for a given input, often formulated via least-squares regression.
concepts.content:
Point prediction occurs when a model outputs just a single prediction $\hat{\mathbf{y}} \in \mathcal{Y}$ for every input $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}$. This is often formulated as least-squares regression, where a function $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ is trained to output a vector of real-valued numbers (such as RGB pixel values) by penalizing the squared distance between the output and the ground truth.

(see figure: Different kinds of predictive distributions.)

Point prediction fails when there are multiple equally valid answers. For example, colorizing a grayscale image is a many-to-one mapping; a single grayscale value could correspond to many different color values. Because a point estimate can only predict one of these multiple possible solutions, it is a poor inference method for fundamentally ambiguous problems.
concepts.motivation_md: Point prediction is the simplest form of regression, but it is insufficient for complex, real-world tasks where data is ambiguous or multimodal.
concepts.recap_md: - Point prediction outputs a single value $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ for a given input $\mathbf{x}$.

slots.motivation: Point prediction is the simplest form of regression, but it is insufficient for complex, real-world tasks where data is ambiguous or multimodal.

concepts.title: Multimodal Distributions in Prediction
concepts.one_liner: Point predictions fail in multimodal distributions by 'splitting the difference' between valid modes, often resulting in impossible outputs.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Different kinds of predictive distributions.)

In ambiguous problems like colorization, the true data distribution $p_{\texttt{data}}$ may be multimodal. For instance, a shirt might be either teal or pink with equal probability. Least-squares regression results in a model that predicts the mean of the data distribution. In this case, the point prediction would be gray—a color that has zero probability under the true data distribution. 

While a point prediction $\hat{a} = f_{\theta}(l)$ can be interpreted as a predictive distribution $p_{\theta}(A = a | l) = \delta(a - \hat{a})$ using the Dirac delta function, it remains fundamentally limited. Even using different loss functions like $L_1$ will not solve the problem, because a single point prediction can only ever represent one mode, whereas the true distribution may have multiple equally probable modes.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the failure of point predictions on multimodal data motivates the need for models that can represent multiple possible outcomes simultaneously.
concepts.recap_md: - Least-squares regression predicts the mean, which may have zero probability in multimodal data.

concepts.title: Predictive Distribution Modeling
concepts.one_liner: Predictive distribution modeling improves on point estimates by predicting the parameters of a probability distribution rather than a single value.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Different kinds of predictive distributions.)

Instead of a point estimate, we can predict a distribution. For example, a least-squares regression model can be viewed as outputting the mean of a Gaussian fit to $p_{\theta}(A | l)$. By also predicting the variance, we obtain a better sense of possible outcomes, though a single Gaussian remains unimodal. 

To capture bimodal or complex data, we can predict the parameters of a more expressive parametric family, such as a mixture of Gaussians. For a mixture of $N$ Gaussians, the model outputs $3N$ numbers: the mean, variance, and weight for each component. The loss function is then the data likelihood under the mixture parameterized by these outputs.
concepts.motivation_md: Predicting a distribution allows a model to express uncertainty and handle multiple possible outcomes that a single point prediction cannot capture.
concepts.recap_md: - Models can output parameters (like mean and variance) of a distribution instead of a single point.

concepts.title: Categorical Distribution for Expressive Predictions
concepts.one_liner: The categorical distribution provides a highly expressive way to model multimodal predictions by quantizing the output space.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Different kinds of predictive distributions.)

The categorical distribution, $\texttt{Cat}$, is a common choice for modeling expressive, multimodal distributions. Because it applies to discrete variables, the output values must first be quantized into bins. For example, an $a$-value in color space can be quantized into ten bins, making the categorical distribution a ten-dimensional vector of non-negative numbers that sum to 1. This parameterization is powerful because all probability mass functions over $k$ classes are members of the family $\texttt{Cat}(k)$, allowing the model to represent any number of modes up to the resolution of the quantization.
concepts.motivation_md: Quantizing continuous outputs into categories allows us to use standard classification tools to model complex, multi-peaked probability distributions without assuming a specific functional form like a Gaussian.
concepts.recap_md: - Categorical distributions require quantizing continuous output values into discrete bins.

concepts.title: Softmax Regression and Expressive Distributions
concepts.one_liner: Softmax regression is a ubiquitous tool because it models a maximally expressive predictive distribution over a quantized space.
concepts.content: Softmax regression is a critical application of the categorical distribution. It is a ubiquitous modeling tool because it models a maximally expressive predictive distribution over a quantized decision space, which explains its effectiveness in classification tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing classification through the lens of generative modeling explains why softmax is so effective: it doesn't just pick a label, it models the most flexible possible distribution over the available choices.
concepts.recap_md: - Softmax regression utilizes the categorical distribution for maximum expressivity in discrete spaces.

concepts.title: Conditional Variational Autoencoders (cVAEs)

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: A conditional VAE (cVAE) defines a conditional distribution as a marginal over latent variables that are independent of the conditioning inputs.
concepts.content:
A variational autoencoder (VAE) is an infinite mixture model based on the identity $p_{	heta}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{	heta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})d\mathbf{z}$. Analogously, any conditional distribution can be defined as the marginal over some latent variable: $p_{	heta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{	heta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x})d\mathbf{z}$. In conditional VAEs (cVAEs), we restrict our attention to latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ that are independent of the inputs we are conditioning on, resulting in the cVAE likelihood model: $$p_{	heta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{	heta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})d\mathbf{z}$$

This corresponds to the following graphical model:
[FIGURE:184e45370a8359cb | A directed acyclic graph (DAG) representing a conditional generative model. It consists of three circular nodes: $X$ and $Z$ at the top, and $Y$ at the bottom. Directed arrows point from $X$ to $Y$...]

The idea is that $\mathbf{z}$ should only encode information about $\mathbf{y}$ that is independent from what $\mathbf{x}$ already provides. For example, in predicting the next frame of a bouncing billiard ball from a single frame $\mathbf{x}$, the color and rough position are known from $\mathbf{x}$, but the velocity is missing. If the model learns to interpret $\mathbf{z}$ as velocity, it achieves a high-likelihood prediction. Just like regular VAEs, cVAEs use an encoder to predict the optimal importance sampling distribution $p_{\theta}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})$. In practice, the encoder takes both $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ as input, and the decoder takes both $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{x}$.

(see figure: A scenario where a yellow ball is moving across a plane. The observation, $\mathbf{x}$, is a static frame. From that observation, we know what will be the color and rough position of the ball in the...)

(see figure: cVAE architecture. The dotted lines indicate that the *target encoder* is only used during training; at test time, usage follows the solid path.)
concepts.motivation_md: cVAEs allow for generative modeling when we have specific conditioning information (like a class label or a previous video frame). They solve the problem of modeling the remaining uncertainty in a prediction by using latent variables to capture only the information not already provided by the conditioning input.
concepts.recap_md: - cVAEs model $p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})$ by marginalizing over a latent variable $\mathbf{z}$ that is independent of the input $\mathbf{x}$.

concepts.title: Conditional Autoregressive Models

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Conditional autoregressive models treat conditioning inputs as a prefix to the sequence of values being modeled.
concepts.content: Autoregressive models already model a sequence of conditional distributions. To condition them on some inputs $\mathbf{x}$, we can simply concatenate $\mathbf{x}$ as a prefix to the sequence of $y$ values we are modeling, yielding the new sequence: $[x_1, \ldots, x_m, y_1, \ldots, y_n]$. The probability model factorizes as: $$p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) = \prod_{i=1}^n p_{\theta}(y_i \bigm | y_1, \ldots, y_{i-1}, x_1, \ldots, x_m)$$ Each distribution in this product is a prediction of the next item in a sequence given the previous items, which is no different than what we had for unconditional autoregressive models. Therefore, the tools for modeling unconditional autoregressive distributions are also appropriate for modeling conditional autoregressive distributions. From an implementation perspective, the same exact code will handle both cases, just depending on whether you prefix the sequence or not.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach allows standard sequence-to-sequence modeling (like translation or text-to-speech) to use the same architectural foundations as unconditional language models by simply prepending the context.
concepts.recap_md: - Conditioning is achieved by concatenating the input $\mathbf{x}$ as a prefix to the target sequence $\mathbf{y}$.

concepts.title: Conditional Diffusion Models

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Conditional diffusion models incorporate conditioning variables by concatenating them into the input of the denoising function.
concepts.content:
Diffusion models can be made conditional by concatenating the conditioning variables, $\mathbf{x}$, into the input to the denoising function: $$\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{t-1} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}_t, t, \mathbf{x})$$ Both diffusion models and autoregressive models convert generative modeling into a sequence of supervised prediction problems. To make them conditional is therefore just as easy as conditioning a supervised learner on more observations. If the original training pairs are $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, we can condition on additional paired observations $\mathbf{c}$ by augmenting the pairs to become $\{[\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{c}^{(i)}], \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. 

An example where we condition on text is shown in (see figure: Text-conditional diffusion model.). The intuition is that if we give $f_{\theta}$ a description of the image as an additional input, then it can do a better job at solving its prediction task. Because of this, $f_{\theta}$ will become sensitive to the text command, and if you give different text it will denoise toward a different image that matches that text.
concepts.motivation_md: Conditional diffusion models enable tasks like text-to-image synthesis by allowing the denoising process to be guided by external information, ensuring the generated output aligns with specific user requirements.
concepts.recap_md: - Conditioning is implemented by adding the context $\mathbf{x}$ as an input to the denoising function $f_{\theta}$.

concepts.title: Structured Prediction in Vision
concepts.one_liner: Structured prediction in vision involves predicting high-dimensional, structured objects like label maps, depth maps, or meshes from an input image.
concepts.content: Whenever you want to make a prediction of an image, conditional generative models are a suitable modeling choice. While image colorization is a classic example, most problems in vision involve predicting labels or geometry. In image classification, the output might be a single class, but in object detection and semantic segmentation, we want a label for each part of the image. The target output in these problems is high-dimensional and structured. Similarly, in geometry estimation, the output is a depth map, a voxel grid, or a mesh. All these are high-dimensional structured objects. The tool needed for solving these problems is structured prediction, and conditional generative models are therefore a good choice for these tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard classification or regression is insufficient for tasks where the output has internal spatial or structural dependencies, such as segmentation or 3D reconstruction. Structured prediction frameworks handle these complex outputs.
concepts.recap_md: - Vision tasks like segmentation and depth estimation require predicting high-dimensional, structured outputs.

concepts.title: Image-to-Image Translation
concepts.one_liner: Image-to-image translation is the problem of mapping an input image to an output image, effectively translating between different views of data.
concepts.content: Image-to-image problems are mapping problems where the input is an image and the output is also an image, defined here as any array of size $N \times M \times C$ (height by width by number of channels). These problems are very common in computer vision and include examples such as colorization, next frame prediction, depth map estimation, and semantic segmentation. One way to think about all these problems is as translating from one view of the data to another. For example, semantic segmentation is a translation from viewing the world in terms of its colors to viewing the world in terms of its semantics. This perspective defines the problem of image-to-image translation, analogous to translating between languages like English and French.
concepts.motivation_md: Many vision tasks can be unified under a single framework where the goal is to transform one representation of a scene (like a sketch or a label map) into another (like a photo).
concepts.recap_md: - Defines vision tasks as a mapping from an input image array to an output image array.

concepts.title: Image-to-Image Translation with a Conditional GAN
concepts.one_liner: Image-to-image translation can be performed using a conditional GAN where a generator maps an input image to an output image and a discriminator evaluates the result.
concepts.content:
One approach to image-to-image translation is to use a conditional GAN, as popularized by the "pix2pix" method. For example, in translating a facade layout map into a photo, the conditioning information (input) is a semantic segmentation image, and the output is a matching photo. The generator maps an image to an image using an architecture like a U-Net (a CNN with skip connections). The discriminator maps the output image to a real-versus-synthetic scalar score using a regular CNN. 

(see figure: The pix2pix @pix2pix2017 model applied to translating a facade layout map into a photo of the facade. The model was trained on the CMP Facades Database @Tylecek13 and the input and ground truth...)

In this setting, noise inputs are often omitted because the input image $\mathbf{x}$ has enough entropy to create variety, though this means the model typically produces only one prediction $\mathbf{y}$ for each input $\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Conditional GANs provide a powerful framework for generating realistic, high-resolution images that are strictly constrained by an input structure, such as a map or a sketch.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses a U-Net generator to map input images to output images and a CNN discriminator for scoring.

concepts.title: GAN Discriminator as a Learned Loss Function
concepts.one_liner: The discriminator of a conditional GAN can be viewed as a learned loss function that adapts to penalize relevant errors made by the generator.
concepts.content:
The setup of a conditional GAN can be viewed as a regression problem with a learned loss function $d_{\phi}$. This loss function adapts to the structure of the data and the behavior of the generator to penalize just the relevant errors the generator is currently making. To stabilize the optimization process, it can be helpful to add a conventional regression loss, such as the $L_1$ loss, to the objective: $$\arg\min_G\max_D \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})) + \left\lVert g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert_1 \big]$$

(see figure: The discriminator of a GAN as a learned loss function.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard losses like Mean Squared Error often produce blurry results in image generation; a learned discriminator loss can capture complex, high-level features of 'realness' that are hard to define mathematically.
concepts.recap_md: - The discriminator acts as a dynamic loss function that penalizes specific generator errors.

concepts.title: PatchGAN Discriminator
concepts.one_liner: A PatchGAN discriminator scores individual image patches as real or fake and averages these scores to determine the total loss.
concepts.content: The architecture of the learned loss function $d_{\phi}$ determines what kinds of errors it penalizes. A popular architecture for image-to-image tasks is the PatchGAN discriminator, which scores each patch in the output image as real or fake and takes the average over patch scores as the total loss: $$d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{i=0}^N \sum_{j=0}^M d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}(\mathbf{x}[i:i+k,j:j+k], \mathbf{y}[i:i+k,j:j+k])$$ where $k \times k$ is the patch size. This operation is equivalent to the sliding window action of a CNN, so $d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}$ can be implemented as a CNN that outputs a $2 \times N \times M$ feature map of real-versus-synthetic scores. Patches can be sampled at different strides and resolutions depending on the CNN architecture.
concepts.motivation_md: By focusing on local patches rather than the whole image, PatchGAN encourages high-frequency detail and texture realism while reducing the number of parameters in the discriminator.
concepts.recap_md: - Scores local $k \times k$ patches to enforce local consistency and high-frequency detail.

slots.key_passage: - Scores local $k \times k$ patches to enforce local consistency and high-frequency detail.

concepts.title: PatchGAN Properties
concepts.one_liner: PatchGAN discriminators offer statistical advantages by modeling local patches rather than entire images, requiring fewer parameters while training on more data samples.
concepts.content:
The PatchGAN strategy has two advantages over just scoring the whole image as real or synthetic with a classifier architecture: (1) it can be easier to model if a patch is real or synthetic than to model if an entire image is real or synthetic ($d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}$ needs fewer parameters), (2) there are more patches in the training data than there are images. These two properties give PatchGAN discriminators a statistical advantage over whole image discriminators (fewer parameters fit to more data). 

The disadvantage is that the PatchGAN only has the architectural capacity to penalize errors that are observable within a single patch. This can be seen by training models with different discriminator patch sizes and observing the results. 

(see figure: Varying the receptive field (patch size) of the convolutional discriminator affects what kinds of structure the discriminator enforces. These results are from @pix2pix2017)

A $1\times1$ discriminator can only observe a single pixel at a time and cannot penalize errors in joint pixel statistics such as edge structure, hence the blurry results. Larger receptive fields can enforce higher order patch realism, but cannot model structure larger than the patch size (hence the tiling artifacts that occur with a period roughly equal to the patch size). Quality degrades with the $286\times286$ discriminator possibly because this discriminator has too hard a task given the limited training data (in any given training set, there are fewer examples of $286\times286$ regions than there are of, say, $70\times70$ regions).
concepts.motivation_md: Whole-image discriminators often require massive parameter counts and struggle with limited data. PatchGAN solves this by focusing on local patches, which increases the effective number of training examples and simplifies the modeling task, allowing the network to focus on high-frequency details like texture and local structure.
concepts.recap_md: - PatchGANs use fewer parameters and more training samples by treating each image patch as a separate data point.

concepts.title: Unpaired Image-to-Image Translation
concepts.one_liner: Unpaired image-to-image translation maps images between domains without requiring direct training pairs of corresponding images.
concepts.content:
In image-to-image translation, we can treat the task like a supervised regression problem using a learned loss function given by a GAN discriminator. This approach works well when we have lots of training data pairs $\{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\}$ to learn from. Unfortunately, very often, paired training data is hard to obtain. For example, consider the task of translating a photo into a Cezanne painting:

(see figure: A style transfer example from the CycleGAN paper @CycleGAN2017 *Input photo source*: Alexei A. Efros.)

This task requires predicting what a scene would look like if a specific artist had painted it. We cannot solve this with paired training data because such data is extremely hard to come by; we would need the artist to paint new scenes for every photo in our training set. However, humans can imagine the answer because we know the artist's style and can reason about the changes needed to make a photo match that style, even without seeing them paired with the exact same scenes. This setting is called the unpaired translation setting, distinguished from paired translation as indicated in the figure below.

(see figure: (left) An example of paired image-to-image translation (colorization) versus (right) unpaired translation (photo to Cezanne). Figure adapted from @CycleGAN2017)
concepts.motivation_md: In many real-world scenarios, such as style transfer or domain adaptation, it is impossible or prohibitively expensive to collect exact pairs of corresponding images (e.g., a photo and its exact oil painting equivalent). Unpaired translation allows models to learn these mappings using independent sets of images from each domain.
concepts.recap_md: - Unpaired translation eliminates the need for one-to-one training pairs $\{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\}$.

concepts.title: Emergent Pairing in GANs
concepts.one_liner: In GANs, the specific mapping between input vectors and output data is not predetermined but emerges during training to satisfy the objective.
concepts.content: GANs have a very useful property well-suited to unpaired translation. They train a mapping from a noise distribution to a data distribution $p(Z) \rightarrow p(X)$. They do this without knowing the pairing between $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{x}$ values in the training data. Instead, this pairing is emergent. Which $\mathbf{z}$-vector corresponds to which $\mathbf{x}$ is not predetermined but self-organizes to satisfy the GAN objective: all $\mathbf{z}$-vectors should map to realistic images, and collectively they should map to the data distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: Because GANs naturally learn to map one distribution to another without explicit supervision of which input maps to which output, they are inherently capable of discovering structure in data where explicit labels or pairs are missing.
concepts.recap_md: - GANs learn a mapping $p(Z) \rightarrow p(X)$ without explicit pairing between individual samples.

concepts.title: Unpaired Learning with GANs
concepts.one_liner: GANs can learn to map between two image domains without paired supervision by matching the output distribution to the target domain.
concepts.content:
Consider training a GAN to map from $\mathbf{x}$ to $\mathbf{y}$ values:

$$\begin{aligned}    \arg\min_{\theta}\max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}(\mathbf{y})) \big]
\end{aligned}$$

This is a regular GAN objective where $\mathbf{y}$ plays the role of the target data and $\mathbf{x}$ plays the role of the noise input. Such a GAN self-organizes so that outputs are realistic $\mathbf{y}$ values and different inputs map to different outputs to collectively match the data distribution over $\mathbf{y}$. No paired supervision is required.

While such a GAN may learn the correct mapping, there are many symmetries in this learning problem. Many different mappings achieve equivalent loss; for example, a permutation of the mapping (shifting which $\mathbf{x}$ maps to which $\mathbf{y}$) achieves the same loss because the GAN objective only cares about the output distribution, not the specific instance-level mapping.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard GAN objectives focus on distribution matching. This allows for learning transformations between domains without pairs, but it introduces the problem of 'identifiability'—the model might learn a valid-looking mapping that is semantically incorrect because many different mappings can produce the same output distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Unpaired GANs match the distribution of outputs to the target domain without needing specific $\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{y}$ pairs.

concepts.title: Set-level vs Instance-level Supervision
concepts.one_liner: GANs utilize set-level supervision by checking if an output belongs to an admissible set rather than matching a specific target instance.
concepts.content:
The GAN discriminator differs from a normal loss function. Rather than checking if the output matches a target instance (that $g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})$ matches $\mathbf{y}^{(i)}$), it checks if the output is part of an admissible set—the set of things that look like realistic $\mathbf{y}$ values. This property makes GANs perfect for working with unpaired data, where we don't have instance-level supervision but only have set-level supervision.

We call this unpaired learning rather than unsupervised because we still have supervision in the form of labels indicating which set each datapoint belongs to (i.e., we know whether each image is an $\mathbf{x}$ or a $\mathbf{y}$).
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional supervised learning requires knowing exactly what the output should be for every input. Set-level supervision relaxes this, allowing models to learn from collections of data (like 'photos' and 'paintings') where we know the category but not the specific correspondences.
concepts.recap_md: - Instance-level supervision requires specific target pairs, while set-level supervision only requires knowing which domain a sample belongs to.

concepts.title: Cycle-consistency
concepts.one_liner: Cycle-consistency is the principle that translating an image to a new domain and back should return it to its original state.
concepts.content:
A regular GAN objective applied to mapping from $X$ to $Y$ solves the unpaired translation problem but does not distinguish between the correct mapping and many other mappings that achieve the same output distribution. To break this symmetry, we add constraints like cycle-consistency. The idea is that if we translate from $X$ to $Y$ and then translate back (from $Y$ to $X$), we should arrive where we started. 

In natural language processing, this is known as backtranslation. For example, translating "apple" to French ("pomme") and then back to English should return "apple." Cycle-consistency losses are regularizers that encourage a learned mapping to be roughly one-to-one. The cycle-consistency losses are defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{cyc}}(\mathbf{x};g_{\theta},f_{\psi}) &= \left\lVert\mathbf{x} - f_{\psi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\right\rVert_1\\
    \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{cyc}}(\mathbf{y};g_{\theta},f_{\psi}) &= \left\lVert\mathbf{y} - g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y}))\right\rVert_1
\end{aligned}
$$
concepts.motivation_md: Without cycle-consistency, an unpaired GAN might map an image of a cat to a random image of a dog. Cycle-consistency forces the model to preserve the structural information of the original image so that the transformation can be reversed, effectively narrowing the space of possible mappings to those that are semantically meaningful.
concepts.recap_md: - Cycle-consistency requires that $f(g(x)) \approx x$ and $g(f(y)) \approx y$.

concepts.title: CycleGAN
concepts.one_liner: CycleGAN is a framework for unpaired image-to-image translation that combines adversarial losses with cycle-consistency constraints to learn one-to-one mappings.
concepts.content:
The complete CycleGAN objective combines adversarial losses with cycle-consistency losses:
$$
\begin{aligned}
    \arg\min_{\theta,\psi}\max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}^{Y}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}^{Y}(\mathbf{y})) + \left\lVert\mathbf{x} - f_{\psi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\right\rVert_1 + \\
    \log d_{\phi}^{X}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}^{X}(\mathbf{x})) + \left\lVert\mathbf{y} - g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y}))\right\rVert_1 \big]
\end{aligned}
$$
This model translates from domain $X$ to domain $Y$ and back, ensuring outputs in each domain look realistic according to their respective discriminators and that the mappings are cycle-consistent. 

(see figure: CycleGAN schematic. Figure derived from @CycleGAN2017)

The cycle-consistency losses encourage the translation to be a one-to-one function, reducing the number of valid solutions. This is effective when the true solution is indeed one-to-one. However, symmetries may still exist: if the $X$-to-$Y$ mapping and its inverse are both permuted incorrectly, CycleGAN may still be satisfied despite the mapping being incorrect.
concepts.motivation_md: CycleGAN was developed to enable high-quality image-to-image translation in the absence of paired data. By training two generators and two discriminators simultaneously with a consistency constraint, it successfully captures the style of a target domain while preserving the content of the source domain.
concepts.recap_md: - CycleGAN uses two sets of GAN losses and two cycle-consistency losses to learn bidirectional mappings.

concepts.title: Trend toward General-Purpose Modeling
concepts.one_liner: The current trend in AI is to replace specialized, task-specific systems with general-purpose conditional generative models.
concepts.content: Many problems in vision can be phrased as structured prediction, and conditional generative models provide a unified and simple solution to a diverse array of these problems. A current trend in computer vision and artificial intelligence is to replace bespoke systems for specific kinds of structured prediction—such as object detectors or image captioning systems—with general-purpose conditional generative models. This shift toward general-purpose modeling tools reduces the need for special-purpose systems designed for specific vision tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: Historically, computer vision relied on hand-engineered pipelines for every unique task. Moving toward general-purpose generative models allows for a more unified architecture that can solve many different problems (translation, detection, synthesis) using the same underlying principles and training objectives.
concepts.recap_md: - Conditional generative models are increasingly used as general-purpose tools for various structured prediction tasks.

concepts.title: Quantization Error in Classification
concepts.one_liner: Quantization error occurs when continuous values are mapped to a discrete set of bins, potentially lowering resolution and causing ambiguity between similar values.
concepts.content: Quantization error is a consequence of treating continuous values as discrete classes. For example, in color prediction, true colors like teal and bright pink may be mapped to discrete bins; if the quantization resolution is low, it becomes impossible to distinguish between similar shades that fall into the same bin. This can result in predictions appearing slightly duller than the true data distribution, such as when a bin is colored with the floor of its range. Generally, this error can be mitigated by increasing the number of classes $k$. In image formats with 256 possible values, setting $k=256$ eliminates quantization error entirely.
concepts.motivation_md: Quantization allows us to apply classification techniques to continuous regression problems, but it introduces a trade-off between the number of classes and the precision of the representation.
concepts.recap_md: - Quantization error arises when continuous data is discretized into a finite number of bins.

slots.motivation: Quantization allows us to apply classification techniques to continuous regression problems, but it introduces a trade-off between the number of classes and the precision of the representation.
slots.key_passage: - Quantization error arises when continuous data is discretized into a finite number of bins.

concepts.title: Curse of Dimensionality in Quantization
concepts.one_liner: The number of classes required for quantization grows exponentially with the number of dimensions, making joint pixel prediction computationally astronomical.
concepts.content: While quantizing a single value into $k$ classes is manageable, the approach suffers from the curse of dimensionality when extended to multiple dimensions. To tile a two-dimensional space (like $ab$ color values) while retaining a resolution of $k$ for both dimensions requires $k^2$ classes. (see figure: The funny shape of the $lab$ color gamut is because not every $ab$ value maps to a valid pixel color. When working with predictions over $lab$ color space, we may map $ab$ values that fall outside...) The problem becomes severe when predicting multiple pixels: quantizing the $ab$-values of $N$ pixels requires $k^{2N}$ classes. For a standard $256 \times 256$ resolution image, the number of classes required becomes astronomical.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains why simple classification cannot be directly scaled to high-dimensional outputs like full images without more sophisticated modeling strategies.
concepts.recap_md: - Quantizing $N$ pixels with $k$ resolution levels per dimension requires $k^{2N}$ discrete classes.

slots.motivation: This concept explains why simple classification cannot be directly scaled to high-dimensional outputs like full images without more sophisticated modeling strategies.
slots.key_passage: - Quantizing $N$ pixels with $k$ resolution levels per dimension requires $k^{2N}$ discrete classes.

concepts.title: Conditional Independence Assumption in Prediction
concepts.one_liner: The conditional independence assumption treats each output dimension as independent of others given the input, a common but often inaccurate simplification in image modeling.
concepts.content: To circumvent the curse of dimensionality, models often factorize the joint distribution by making independent predictions for each pixel. This corresponds to the factorization: $$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{ab} \bigm | \mathbf{l}) = \prod_{n=1}^N\prod_{m=1}^M p_{\theta}(ab[n,m,:] \bigm | \mathbf{l}) \end{aligned}$$ This model assumes pixel colors are conditionally independent given the luminance image. This same assumption is implicit in least-squares regression ($L_2$ loss) for multidimensional prediction. Because the $L_2$ loss factorizes as a product over pairwise potentials, the Hammersley-Clifford theorem implies a probability distribution where all true values $y_i$ are independent given the predictions $\hat{y}_i$ (and thus given the input $\mathbf{x}$). While computationally efficient, this assumption is rarely true in computer vision problems.
concepts.motivation_md: Factorizing the joint distribution into independent conditional probabilities makes high-dimensional prediction computationally feasible, though it ignores the structural relationships between output dimensions.
concepts.recap_md: - Conditional independence assumes $p(y_1, y_2 | x) = p(y_1 | x)p(y_2 | x)$. - Least-squares regression ($L_2$ loss) implicitly assumes conditional independence between output dimensions.

slots.motivation: Factorizing the joint distribution into independent conditional probabilities makes high-dimensional prediction computationally feasible, though it ignores the structural relationships between output dimensions.
slots.key_passage: - Conditional independence assumes $p(y_1, y_2 | x) = p(y_1 | x)p(y_2 | x)$. - Least-squares regression ($L_2$ loss) implicitly assumes conditional independence between output dimensions.
slots.example: To circumvent the curse of dimensionality, models often factorize the joint distribution by making independent predictions for each pixel. This corresponds to the factorization: $$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{ab} \bigm | \mathbf{l}) = \prod_{n=1}^N\prod_{m=1}^M p_{\theta}(ab[n,m,:] \bigm | \mathbf{l}) \end{aligned}$$ This model assumes pixel colors are conditionally independent given the luminance image. This same assumption is implicit in least-squares regression ($L_2$ loss) for multidimensional prediction. Because the $L_2$ loss factorizes as a product over pairwise potentials, the Hammersley-Clifford theorem implies a probability distribution where all true values $y_i$ are independent given the predictions $\hat{y}_i$ (and thus given the input $\mathbf{x}$). While computationally efficient, this assumption is rarely true in computer vision problems.

concepts.title: Unstructured Prediction
concepts.one_liner: Unstructured prediction refers to fitting models that assume independence between output dimensions, such as pixels, conditioned on the input.
concepts.content: Unstructured prediction occurs when using methods like per-pixel classification or least-squares regression that implicitly assume independence between all output pixels, conditioned on the input.
concepts.motivation_md: Identifying unstructured prediction helps researchers understand why certain models fail to capture global coherence or spatial relationships in complex outputs.
concepts.recap_md: - Unstructured prediction assumes independence between output components given the input.

concepts.title: Color Flipping in Unstructured Prediction
concepts.one_liner: Color flipping is a failure in unstructured prediction where independent pixel choices cause chaotic transitions between colors in regions of uncertainty.
concepts.content: Color flipping occurs when an unstructured classifier makes independent hard decisions for each pixel in a multi-modal distribution. If a model learns roughly equal probabilities for two modes (e.g., teal and pink), slight changes in input luminance can cause the prediction to wiggle between these modes. Because choices are made independently per pixel, the output may chaotically alternate between colors. (see figure: Color flipping can arise from a smooth underlying predictive distribution, on top of which independent choices are made.) A real example from @zhang2016colorful shows a model alternating between blue and red for a shirt and background because it is unsure of the correct color. concepts.title: Structured Prediction

position.section_title: Conditional Generative Models Solve Multimodal Structured Prediction

concepts.one_liner: Structured prediction methods model the joint structure of the output space rather than factorizing it into independent potentials.
concepts.content: Structured prediction methods model joint structure in the output space and do not factorize the output into independent potentials conditioned on the input. Conditional generative modeling is a structured prediction approach that models a full distribution of possibilities over the joint configuration of outputs.
concepts.motivation_md: Structured prediction is necessary for tasks where the output components (like pixels in an image) are highly correlated and must be consistent with one another.
concepts.recap_md: - Structured prediction models the joint distribution of outputs rather than independent components.

concepts.title: Amortized Inference

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Amortized inference uses a neural network to learn a direct mapping from inputs to outputs, distributing the cost of inference over the training phase.
concepts.content: Amortized inference refers to an approach where the cost of inference is amortized over a training phase. A neural network learns a direct mapping from inputs to outputs, approximating the solution that would have been obtained through exact inference on a given input.
concepts.motivation_md: Amortized inference allows for extremely fast predictions at test time by shifting the heavy computational burden to the offline training stage.
concepts.recap_md: - Amortized inference replaces expensive per-instance optimization with a learned mapping function.

concepts.title: Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (cGANs)

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Conditional GANs extend the GAN framework by providing an input to both the generator and discriminator, enabling the modeling of conditional distributions.
concepts.content: A conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) is created by adding an input $\mathbf{x}$ to both the generator and the discriminator: $$\begin{aligned} \arg\min_{\theta}\max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})) \big] \end{aligned}$$ This changes the discriminator's task to determining if the input-output pair $(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})$ is real or synthetic. A pair may be flagged as synthetic if the output itself looks fake or if the output does not match the input. If both conditions are satisfied, the samples produced are $iid$ with respect to the true conditional distribution $p_{\texttt{data}}(Y \bigm | \mathbf{x})$.
concepts.motivation_md: Conditional GANs allow for targeted generation, such as generating an image based on a specific label or a source image, rather than just generating random samples from a dataset.
concepts.recap_md: - cGANs add an auxiliary input $\mathbf{x}$ to the generator and discriminator. - The discriminator evaluates the consistency of the input-output pair.

Quantization error is a direct consequence of the discretization required to use categorical distributions for continuous data.
The curse of dimensionality is a primary scaling limitation when applying categorical quantization to multi-dimensional output spaces.
Unstructured prediction is defined by the use of models that implicitly assume conditional independence between output dimensions.
Color flipping occurs specifically when an unstructured model attempts to predict from a multi-modal distribution.

This technique provides the mechanism for learning translations without paired data.

CycleGAN builds upon the basic unpaired GAN objective by adding consistency constraints.

overlay.rationale: Structured prediction models the joint structure of the output space, whereas unstructured prediction factorizes the output into independent components.
